papers.title: A Spectral Zoo of Genus-Zero Free Boundary Minimal Surfaces with Many Boundary Components
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31936v1

summary.one_liner: A numerical and asymptotic study of critical points of the length-normalized first Steklov eigenvalue on genus-zero surfaces with many boundary components, linking them to free boundary minimal surfaces and free curve limits.
summary.plain: The paper looks at special curved surfaces that sit inside a ball and meet its edge at right angles, and at the "best" versions of them measured by a number tied to how a drum vibrates at its lowest mode. The authors computed 268 such surfaces numerically, with up to 2252 boundary holes, and checked their symmetries and stability. They also describe how families of these surfaces appear to approach simpler limit shapes made of flat disks and catenoid-like tubes, and give an estimate of the limiting value for large numbers of holes.
summary.why: It gives a large, numerically certified catalogue of candidate extremal surfaces and connects them to explicit limit shapes, which may help map out the landscape of free boundary minimal surfaces. How far the numerical picture holds in general is not settled by the text: the large-b asymptotic is described as a formal evaluation, and the families are said to "appear" to converge.
summary.background:
- Minimal surface: a surface with zero mean curvature, locally shaped like a soap film.
- Free boundary minimal surface: a minimal surface inside a ball whose edge lies on the sphere and meets it at right angles.
- Steklov eigenvalue: a vibration-type number attached to a surface's boundary, measuring how a harmonic function's energy leaks out through the edge; the first one is the lowest nontrivial such value.
- Length normalization: rescaling by the boundary length so the number does not depend on the size of the surface.
- Critical point: a shape where small changes do not change the value to first order; the Morse index counts the directions in which it can be decreased.
- Uniformization: mapping a surface conformally onto a standard shape, here a sphere with round caps removed.
- Catenoid: the tube-like minimal surface formed by a soap film between two rings.
- Logarithmic energy: a standard quantity from potential theory measuring how points repel each other through a logarithm of distance.

papers.abstract: We study critical points of the length-normalized first Steklov eigenvalue $\bar\sigma_1$ on genus-zero surfaces with $b$ boundary components. By a theorem of Fraser and Schoen, their first eigenfunctions give free boundary minimal surfaces in the unit ball. After uniformization, the domain is the round sphere minus $b$ round caps, with a weight on the boundary circles. A layer potential formulation gives the eigenvalues, their derivatives and a certificate for each critical point, and an exact multipole system for the caps. We compute a spectral zoo of 268 numerically certified critical points with up to $b=2252$ boundary components, including the $27$ embedded examples listed by Schulz. With their symmetry groups and Morse indices, the critical points satisfy a signed count for $3\le b\le10$. Most belong to families built from rings of boundary components. As the rings fill in, these appear to converge to the free curve minimal surfaces of Karpukhin and Noutchegueme, unions of flat disks and catenoidal annuli that meet along circles on the sphere. We construct these limits, among them the critical drum and the cake stand, a flat disk with a catenoidal horn. The families approach their limits like $j^{-1}$ for rings of $j$ caps, and the equatorial family approaches $4\pi$ with deficit $4\pi b^{-1}e^{-b}$. For large $b$, the leading terms of the multipole system reduce to the logarithmic energy of the cap centers and a formal evaluation gives $\bar\sigma_1^\star(b)=8\pi-16\pi\,b^{-1}\log b+O(b^{-1})$.

papers.title: Sub-Riemannian Distances on Lie Groups: Tangent Asymptotics and Hermitian Matrix Formulas
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31447v1

summary.one_liner: The paper gives small-scale asymptotics of Carnot–Carathéodory (sub-Riemannian) distance on two-step Lie groups, comparing it to the nilpotent tangent group, with precise error orders and a Hermitian-matrix formula for block subgroups of SU(N).
summary.plain: The paper studies shortest paths in a curved space where only certain directions of motion are allowed, such as steering a vehicle that can only move forward and turn. It asks how the length of these shortest routes behaves when the points are very close to the starting point. The authors show that, for small distances, the squared distance matches a simpler model space up to a known error, and they give explicit formulas for a special family of groups.
summary.why: Sub-Riemannian distances appear in control theory, robotics and the geometry of quantum systems, so precise small-scale approximations can be useful there. The text does not say how the results will be applied elsewhere, so any wider connection is uncertain.
summary.background:
- Lie group: a smooth space with a compatible group multiplication, such as rotations of a body.
- Sub-Riemannian (Carnot–Carathéodory) distance: shortest path length when only some directions of motion are permitted.
- Two-step: the allowed directions generate the full space after one level of brackets (commutators).
- Nilpotent tangent group: a simpler model group that approximates the space near a point.
- Asymptotic expansion: writing a quantity as a main term plus an error term that shrinks at a stated rate as the scale r goes to 0.
- Cut point and abnormal endpoint: places where shortest paths stop being unique or fail to follow the usual rules.
- Hermitian matrix and trace norm: square complex matrices equal to their conjugate transpose, and a standard size measure for them.
- Trigonometric polynomial: a finite sum of sine and cosine terms, here describing a minimizing closed loop.

papers.abstract: Let $d_{\mathrm{SR}}$ be the Carnot--Carath\'{e}odory distance associated with a two-step Lie pair and let $d_0$ be the distance on its nilpotent tangent group. For compact Lie pairs we prove, locally uniformly in $(X,Z)$, \[ d_{\mathrm{SR}}\!\left(e,\exp(rX+r^2Z)\right)^2 =r^2d_0(e,(X,Z))^2+O(r^3). \] For symmetric pairs, the remainder improves to $O(r^4)$. This order is sharp in general, and the estimate remains uniform at cut points, abnormal endpoints, and points where the tangent endpoint map changes rank. If the tangent minimizer is unique, the endpoint differential is onto, and the constrained Hessian is coercive, we determine the coefficient of $r^4$ with remainder $O(r^6)$. For block subgroups of $\mathrm{SU}(N)$, we express the vertical squared distance on the tangent group as the attained minimum of a finite-dimensional functional on Hermitian matrices subject to linear constraints on their partial traces. Every minimizer gives a minimizing loop represented by a trigonometric polynomial. For one $m$-dimensional block and $q$ scalar blocks, the coefficient has weights $\lceil j/q\rceil$ and reduces to a trace norm formula when $q\ge\lfloor m/2\rfloor$.

papers.title: Rotationally symmetric fractional minimal surfaces
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32252v1

summary.background:
- Minimal surface: a surface whose mean curvature is zero, like a soap film spanning a wire frame.
- Mean curvature: a local measure of how a surface bends on average.
- Fractional (s-) version: replaces the local curvature with a nonlocal quantity, weighted by a parameter s between 0 and 1, so distant parts of the surface influence each point.
- Radial set / concentric spheres: regions whose boundaries are nested spheres centered at one point, which makes the problem reduce to one radial variable.
- Rotational symmetry: the shape looks the same when turned around an axis or center.
- Locally finite hypersurface: a surface that, in every bounded region, is made of finitely many pieces.
- Rescaling and limit: shrinking or enlarging a configuration so its innermost radius becomes fixed, then studying what shape the sequence approaches.
summary.one_liner: The paper constructs a rotationally symmetric s-minimal surface, built from alternating radial sets bounded by concentric spheres, in which the fractional mean curvature H_s vanishes at every free interface, and shows that a rescaled limit gives a properly embedded locally finite hypersurface with H_s = 0 on its boundary.
summary.plain: The paper studies a generalized version of a soap-film-like surface, where the usual curvature rule is replaced by a "fractional" rule that depends on the whole shape rather than only on nearby points. The authors build an example of such a surface that has rotational symmetry, made of alternating shells bounded by concentric spheres. They then rescale these shapes and take a limit, obtaining a rotationally symmetric surface that satisfies the fractional rule at every point of its boundary.
summary.why: Explicit non-trivial examples are rare for fractional minimal surfaces, so a concrete rotationally symmetric case gives the theory something to test against. The text does not say what wider applications it may have, so its broader significance is uncertain.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we provide a non-trivial example of an $s$-minimal surface that is invariant under rotations. More precisely, we study alternating radial sets whose boundaries are finite or locally finite unions of concentric spheres and prove that, fixing the outer radius to $r=1$, there exists a radial configuration for which the fractional mean curvature $H_s$ vanishes at every free interface. We then show that rescaling radial maximizers by their innermost radius and passing to the limit yields a properly embedded, rotationally symmetric, locally finite hypersurface satisfying $H_s=0$ at every point of the boundary.

papers.title: An intrinsic criterion for Pansu differentials to be homomorphisms of nilpotent Lie groups
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32893v1

summary.background:
- Lie group: a continuous group of transformations, such as rotations and translations, with smooth structure.
- Nilpotent group: a group whose repeated commutators eventually vanish, making it "almost abelian" in layers.
- Carnot group: a nilpotent group with a graded structure, the model spaces for Pansu's theorem.
- Bracket-generating distribution: a family of allowed directions of motion whose commutators span the whole tangent space, so any two points can be connected by paths along those directions.
- Pansu differential: a limiting linear-like approximation of a Lipschitz map (a map with bounded stretching) at almost every point, which is a group homomorphism when the target is Carnot.
- Grading and step: a decomposition of the Lie algebra into layers; the step is the number of layers needed.
- Homomorphism: a map that preserves the group operation.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives an intrinsic criterion, for a suitable grading, for when the Pansu differential of a Lipschitz map from a nilpotent Lie group with bracket-generating distribution is a group homomorphism, and shows the threshold on target step is sharp.
summary.plain: The paper studies how "smooth-like" maps behave between curved, non-Euclidean spaces built from groups of motions. For a class of such spaces, the best local linear approximation of a map may fail to respect the group structure. The authors identify a condition, phrased using only the space itself, that decides when it does, and show with an example that a size threshold in that condition cannot be loosened.
summary.why: Pansu differentiation is a central tool for understanding maps between sub-Riemannian and metric spaces, so a clean test for when the approximation is a true homomorphism is useful to specialists. The text does not claim wider applications, and I am not certain how far the criterion extends beyond the setting described.

papers.abstract: By Pansu's theorem, Lipschitz maps between Carnot groups are differentiable almost everywhere, and their differentials are group homomorphisms. When the domain is instead a nilpotent Lie group with a bracket-generating left-invariant distribution, the Pansu differential is a homomorphism of an osculating Carnot group, which depends on an auxiliary choice of grading, and it need not be a homomorphism of the original group. We give an intrinsic criterion for when it is one, for a suitable choice of grading: the differential must vanish on an ideal that depends only on the group and its distribution, and comes from a universal quotient onto a Carnot group. The criterion holds automatically when the step of the target is small enough, and an explicit example shows that this threshold is sharp. Along the way, we determine exactly how the obstruction depends on the choice of grading.

papers.title: Cylindrical Ricci flows and the PDE-ODI principle
papers.label: arXiv:2611.29246v1

summary.background:
- Ricci flow: a process that deforms a geometric space over time, shrinking regions of high curvature; it is a central tool in the proof of the Poincaré conjecture.
- Ancient flow: a flow defined for all negative times, i.e. one studied looking backward into the far past.
- Asymptotically cylindrical: the shape looks more and more like a cylinder (a round tube times a line) as one goes back in time.
- Soliton: a special self-similar shape that evolves in a predictable way; a Bryant soliton is a particular steady-type example.
- Asymptotics: precise description of how a quantity behaves in a limit, here the leading correction terms.
- Mean curvature flow: a related geometric evolution of surfaces, whose cylindrical case the authors treated earlier.
- Harmonic map heat flow: a standard PDE tool used here as a coordinate (gauge) choice.
- Ricci flow with surgery: a method of continuing the flow past singularities by cutting and capping; the paper says these tools are aimed at this in dimension 4.
summary.one_liner: The paper derives precise asymptotics for ancient asymptotically cylindrical Ricci flows, showing a linear-or-quadratic dichotomy in the leading deviation from the cylinder, and uses a PDE-ODI principle and a harmonic map heat flow gauge that works without a curvature sign assumption.
summary.plain: This paper studies how a curved shape evolving over time (a Ricci flow, which smooths out a geometric space much like heat spreads through metal) behaves when it looks like a long cylinder in the far past. The authors show that the first correction away from a perfect cylinder is either linear or quadratic in the stretched-out directions. In the linear case, the flow closely matches a known special shape (a Bryant soliton) times a flat Euclidean factor.
summary.why: The results are technical but structural: they give a unified treatment of Ricci flow and mean curvature flow via one shared principle, and the tools are said to be part of a program toward Ricci flow with surgery in dimension 4. The text does not claim wider consequences beyond this.

papers.abstract: We derive precise asymptotics for ancient asymptotically cylindrical Ricci flows. We establish a dichotomy in which the leading deviation from the cylinder is either linear or quadratic in the axial variables. In the linear case, we show that the flow is exponentially asymptotic to a Bryant soliton times a Euclidean factor. For $\kappa$-solutions, we further show that the flow is isometric to such a product, up to parabolic rescaling. In the quadratic case, we obtain higher-order asymptotics governed by a finite-dimensional invariant. We also establish propagation of cylindrical regions and uniqueness of cylindrical tangent flows. These results closely parallel those in our earlier work on cylindrical mean curvature flows. Both analyses use the same PDE-ODI principle and yield a unified treatment of cylindrical Ricci flow and mean curvature flow. The essential new ingredient in the Ricci flow setting is a coherent harmonic map heat flow gauge, which allows us to apply this principle without assuming a sign for the curvature. The local analytic tools developed here also form part of a program aimed at constructing Ricci flow with surgery in dimension 4.

papers.title: Scaling limits for equivariant Szeg\H{o} kernels near a singular point of the moment map and applications to K\"ahler reduction
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30311v1

summary.background:
- Hodge manifold: a complex geometric space with a line bundle whose curvature is positive, so holomorphic sections are well behaved.
- Compact Lie group action: a compact symmetry group acting holomorphically on the space.
- Moment map: a function that encodes the group action; zero being a singular value means the reduction at zero is singular.
- Kähler (symplectic) reduction: forming a quotient space by fixing the moment map level and dividing out the symmetry.
- Szegő kernel: the reproducing kernel for holomorphic sections, which acts as a density-type object in quantization.
- Guillemin–Sternberg map: a map relating quantization before and after reduction.
- Asymptotic unitarity and scaling limits: statements about behaviour as a power of the line bundle grows large, examined after rescaling near a point.
summary.one_liner: Studies scaling limits of equivariant Szegő kernels near a singular point of the moment map for a compact group action on a Hodge manifold, and applies them to the quantization of the singular Kähler reduced space.
summary.plain: This paper looks at a symmetry-based construction in geometry: when a group of symmetries acts on a space, one can build a smaller "reduced" space by keeping only the symmetric parts. The authors study what happens near a special point where this reduction becomes singular (the reduced space is no longer smooth). They use a rescaling technique that zooms in on that point to describe the behaviour of the relevant kernels there.
summary.why: The text describes how the method applies to several questions about invariant sections near singular strata, including whether the Guillemin–Sternberg map stays asymptotically unitary there. Its wider significance beyond this specialist setting is not stated in the text, so I cannot say more about it.

papers.abstract: Suppose that a compact and connected Lie group acts holomorphically on a Hodge manifold, and that the action linearises to the associated Hermitian ample line bundle. Assume that zero is a singular value of the associated moment map. The spaces of global holomorphic sections of powers of the line bundle decompose over the finite dimensional irreducible representations of the group. The main goal of this paper is to study the scaling limits for equivariant Szeg\H{o} kernels near a singular point of the moment map. As an application, we discuss the quantization of the singular reduced space: the behaviour of invariant sections along the singular strata, the failure of the asymptotic unitarity of the Guillemin--Sternberg map near the singular strata, and the number of invariant sections concentrated near a singular orbit.

papers.title: Projectively Flat Spherically Symmetric Sprays of Constant Curvature
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27723v1

summary.background:
- Manifold: a space that looks locally like ordinary Euclidean space, on which calculus can be done.
- Finsler metric: a way of measuring length in which the length of a vector can depend on its direction, generalizing Riemannian metrics.
- Spray: a geometric object on the space of directions that determines the "natural paths" (geodesics) of a Finsler metric.
- Projective flatness: the spray's paths match straight lines up to reparametrization, the Finsler analogue of a flat-looking geometry.
- Spherical symmetry: the spray looks the same in all directions around a point, so it depends only on the radius r and a direction variable s.
- Flag curvature: a measure of how curved the space is along a given 2-dimensional direction; constant means the same everywhere and in all directions.
- Projective factor p(r,s): the function that encodes the spray's projective structure and is solved for in the paper.
summary.one_liner: The paper classifies projectively flat, spherically symmetric sprays of constant curvature by solving the equations that constant curvature imposes on the projective factor p(r,s), obtaining four explicit families that include the spray cases for constant flag curvature K = 0, -1, and 1.
summary.plain: This is a pure mathematics paper about "sprays," which are rules describing how straight-line-like paths behave on a curved space, the kind used in Finsler geometry (a generalization of Riemannian geometry where distances can depend on direction). The authors write down the conditions that make such a spray have constant curvature, solve them, and sort every possible solution into four explicit families. They also check that the known constant-curvature examples with curvature 0, -1, and 1 fall inside these families.
summary.why: The result gives a complete list rather than a set of examples, which matters for anyone studying which curved geometries of this type exist. The text does not describe applications outside geometry, so its wider relevance is uncertain.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we study projectively flat spherically symmetric sprays of constant curvature. We derive a system of equations that is equivalent to the constant-curvature condition for such sprays and solve it to obtain a complete classification of the projective factor \(p(r,s)\) into four explicit families. We further show that the sprays induced by projectively flat spherically symmetric Finsler metrics of constant flag curvature \(K=0\), \(K=-1\), and \(K=1\) are all special cases of our classification, thereby confirming that the sprays induced by these constant-flag-curvature Finsler metrics are fully contained in our framework.

papers.title: A local symmetry forces positivity for projectively induced Kahler-Einstein metrics
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27345v1

summary.background:
- Kähler manifold: a complex geometric space with a compatible notion of distance and angle.
- Kähler–Einstein metric: a Kähler metric whose Ricci curvature is a constant multiple of the metric; the sign of that constant (positive, zero, negative) is the key quantity.
- Projective space and submanifold: the complex analogue of the sphere-like space of lines through the origin; a submanifold is a smaller shape embedded inside it.
- Killing field: a smooth vector field whose flow preserves the metric, i.e. a continuous symmetry.
- Real-holomorphic vector field: a flow that respects the complex structure.
- Calabi rigidity: a result saying that local symmetries of such embeddings extend in a controlled way.
- Omori–Yau maximum principle and Yau's Liouville theorem: standard tools for showing that certain bounded functions on non-compact spaces must be constant.
- Hulin's continuation: a known construction extending the embedded metric; the text uses it as an input.
summary.one_liner: The paper shows that a projectively induced Kähler–Einstein metric must have positive Einstein constant whenever it has at least one nonzero local real-holomorphic Killing field, with no completeness or global group-action assumption, and extends this to a non-Einstein obstruction and compact equivariant continuations.
summary.plain: The paper studies curved geometric shapes that sit inside a flat-style projective space and carry a specific kind of balanced, evenly curved structure. The authors show that if such a shape has even a local symmetry (a smooth flow that preserves the geometry in a neighbourhood), then its curvature must be strictly positive, so negative and zero curvature are ruled out. The argument uses a global extension of the local symmetry, which the text describes as coming from a known rigidity result of Calabi.
summary.why: The general question of whether such embedded Kähler–Einstein submanifolds of projective space must have positive curvature is open, and this gives a partial answer under a local symmetry hypothesis. The text does not say how far the method extends beyond this setting, so its wider reach is uncertain.

papers.abstract: We prove that a projectively induced Kahler-Einstein metric has positive Einstein constant as soon as it admits one nonzero local real-holomorphic Killing field. Neither completeness nor a prescribed global group action is assumed. This gives a partial answer, under a local symmetry hypothesis, to the general positivity problem for Kahler-Einstein submanifolds of (finite-dimensional) projective space. The key observation is that, by Calabi rigidity, a local real-holomorphic Killing field is induced by a projective unitary vector field whose tangency propagates along any connected global Kahler immersion, without a simple-connectivity assumption. Applied to Hulin's complete continuation, this produces a global Killing field with a bounded Hamiltonian potential given by the ambient projective moment map. The resulting Laplace equation, the Omori--Yau maximum principle and Yau's Liouville theorem exclude both negative and zero Einstein curvature. We also prove a non-Einstein obstruction under uniformly negative Ricci curvature and obtain compact equivariant continuations.
